(Family Letter No. 7)
En route Beirut to Cairo
March 16, 1950
Dear Family,
We left Bangkok on the 14th, flew to Calcutta for a re-
fueling stop and then he ded for Delhi, our next scheduled port of
call, but we didn't get there.
A thunderstorm at Delhi put the
ground radio station
out of commission so we landed instead at
Allahabad on the way between Delhi and Calcutta.
There we stayed
from about midnight until eight o'clock in the morning. I did not
say anything to Debby and Hebe abnut it but I was a little worried
during the night because we had fifteen Moslems on board who were
fleeing from India to Pakistan (Karachi).
Allahabad is in India
the Hindus would have just loved to club the Moslems to death.
However, none of the Moslems left the eirplane and no mob showed up.
We took off at 8:00 a.m. and arrived Delhi an hour and forty minutes
There we had breakfast, then took off for Karachi, Pakistan
where we dropped off our Moslem refugees.
Soon we were flying out
over the Indian Ocean along the rocky, forbidding coast of Iran.
You probably recall the recent visit
of the Shah of Iran to the
United States.
He was visiting Karachi when we landed there.
Pakistan people were making quite a show of his visit, and the road
to town was lined with Pakistan Moslem troops. No doubt they want
the support of Iran in the not unlikely event of war with India.
As I told you in a previous letter, the new government of Pakistan
is devoting 80% of its national income to military expenditures.
Their hard-won "independence", like th t of the Philippines has not
brought all the predicted blessings.
In fact, in India it has
brought death to millions, while other millions have been forced to
flee from their homes and take up a penniless life anew in a strange
country.
We did not leave the airport but a passenger who boarded
our plane at Karachi said that there were pictures of the Shah of
Iran all over town and at one point a huge arch over the road which
leads north with a sign "Gateway to Kashmir", that province claimed
by both Indis and Pekistan which may lead to civil war between the
two countries.
Back in 1942 I met the Shah of Iran under rather amusing
circumstances. A military friend of mine in Washington asked
me
to show a Mr. Pahlevy around LaGuardia end our shops there. We had
lunch together, quite informally, and a plessant tour of the airport
during the course of which we ran into a couple of Generals of the
Iranian Army who had flown up from Washington to meet "Mr. Pahlevy".
When they did so, they both fell on their knees and bumped their heads
Then I learned for the first time th t "Mr. Pahlevy"
le flew up the Persian Gulf past fabulous Kuwait and the
Neutral Territory which is owned 50-50 by Saudi Arabia and Kuwait to
Basra in the southeast part of Iraq at the head of the Persian Gulf,
see map enclosed. There we landed for refueling and a few passengers
and then went on at night across Saudi Arabia to Damascus where we
arrived at ten p.m. Until the pipelines mere built across the desert

to the "editerranean, Basra was one of the principal ports of call
for tankers and was especialiy important during the war when the
"Desert Fox" Rommel all but closed the Mediterranean and the Suez
Canal to allied shipping. Kuwait is a most interesting and little
known Sheikdom. It has
recently become such an important oil source
that P.A.A. is seeking authority from the C.A.B. to land there.
Sheik (pronounced Shake) now has an income of $80,000 per day in oil
royalties or •20¢ per barrel from 400,000 barrels of oil. He lives
in a rather glorified mud house in a small village of the same con-
struction.
His one extravagance is a big Packard presented to him
by one of the oil companies and a rather well-stocked harem of his
own selection.
The people of Kuwait heretofore and even now thrive
on gold. The latter is flown into Kuwait from ell over the world.
In fact, the airline on which we are now flying, which is one-third
owned by P.A.A., does a big business in the transport of gold to
Kuwait. All is perfectly legal until the gold arrives there.
the dhows, that picturesque type of vessel with a triangular sail,
carry the gold down the Persian Gulf and across the Indian Ocean
There in some secluded bay or inlet the gold
is smuggled into India. Fach of these strange craft may carry as
much as $500,000-worth of gold. Probably the skipper is the only
man on board who can read or write but the twenty man crew all share
in the profits and are quite reliable and honest according to their
lights.
Just what the Sheik will do with all his oil money is an
unknown question.
Cairo
Merch 17, 1950
Middle East Airlines, on which es I
said above, we flew
here from Beirut, is an interesting company. It is owned as to
about 66% by Lebanon businessmen and the balance by P.A.A.
The
chief pilot is an Englishman and most of the pilots are Romaniens
whohave escaped from behind the iron curtain.
Our pilot was one
of them and did a good job of flying our DC-3. We flew along the
coast of much publicized Israel, well out to sea, past the ancient
biblical city of Tyre, then Haifa, Tel Aviv and on down to Port Said,
where the Suez Canal enters the Mediterranean.

Then on across the
flat delta of the Nile to the airport for Coiro at Heliopolis. We
drove into Cairo with the P.A.A. representative, had lunch st
Shepherds and then drove out to Mena House in the shadow of Cheops,
largest of the pyramids. We took a walk over to the pyramids end
the Sphinx, had an early dinner and turned in.
This morning we had
breadfast in our room looking out on the pyrinids and the desert.
After breakfast we again went over to the pyramids, this
time with a guide,
or dragoman, who told us all about them.
boarded camels in front of the Sphinx for the enclosed picture. Our
dragoman is the over-exposed Caesar with his "toga" thrown over his
shoulder.
Ve became very attached to him.
The camel is a strange
beast. He perpetually wears & supercilious, snooty sneer like the
most up-stage of Newport hostesses who smells something bad. He has
many good charecteristies and, like most of us, some bad ones. Pro-
minent among the latter is an uncontrollable and unpredictable urge
to take a bite out of the men who leads him. Just before going into

-3-
this act he lets out with a. loud throat noise which is somewhere
between a cough and a sneeze.
In Shanghai we knew a certain titled
resident who made a small fortune on opium and a big one on Shanghai
real estate.
He built a marble palace which occupied a whole city
block.
The ballroom was the size of a tennis court and had so many
lights in it that when he turned them all on everyone in Shanghai
knew it.
He used to give enormous parties, but one of our British
friends claimed that Sir Robert got his pre-opium start as a Bagdad
Jew and that he was more at home leading camels than cotillions.
In fact, our British friend claimed that at one huge reception when
Sir Robert was heading the receiving line our said British friend,
(who had served under Lawrence of Arabia and knew his camels) after a
few scotch and sodas, slid around behind Sir Robert and made a noise
like a camel.
According to his story, Sir Robert jumped half way
across the ballroom.
Well - to forget this diversion and get on
with my story: Debby's camel was called "Brooklyn Bridge", Hebe's
was "Canada Dry" (she took a close-up of him for Gordon) and mine
was "Missouri" and plenty beat up, too! Hebe's kept making funny
noises in his throat which did not. add to her comfort already reduced
to an all-time low.
We rode the camels about half a mile back to
our car, convinced that air transportation is safer, faster more
comfortable and not so expensive! Then we drove into Cairo, toured
the old city, had lunch at the Hotel. Semiramis and in the afternoon
visited a couple of Mosques and the bazaar.
Saturday
March 18, 1950
This morning we drove out to Sakkara, the burying ground
for ancient Memphis.
The Egyptian Government is doing some excavation
and restoration work there, but our dragoman, Ashour Aboul Kerim, in
typical native form said there was so much steeling going on that the
work has been curtailed. In common with most Arabs and Egyptians he
has confidence only in British or American archeologists.
in to the Mena House for lunch and in the afternoon to the Barrage
Islands - a series of dems and locks which completely control the
four outlets of the Nile so that the water-table can be kept exactly
where they want it throughout the vast and fertile delta. In the
old days the river overflowed every year and for a period of three
months the whole great delta was under water. It was during these
three months that all the stones for the pyramids were ferried from
the quarries on the east side to the base of the pyramids on the west
In fact, our dragoman pictured old Cheops - builder of the
Great Pyramid - as a sort of ancient F.D.R. who created a Public Works
Administration to give the farmers work during the months when their
fields were inundated, but I suspect that Cheops did not provide
shovels with crutch-top handles to lean on !
Sunday
March 19, 1950
This morning we went to the Cairo Museum and ended up, of
course, at the Tutankhamun exhibit which even the Hollywood phrase-
makers
would find difficult to superlative.
You will no doubt re-
member the description of the tomb with its four gold-covered shrines
nestled one within the other.
The inner coffin of solid gold weighs
243 pounds. It is truly remarkable that this tomb was not looted by

a charming Inn on the edge of the Lake. During lunch a strolling

voice and a guitar sang French
and Italian songs.
we thought he must be an ex-Italian P.o.w. but
he told us that he was from Lebanon.
The latter country interests
us very much. It seems to be the most up and coming nation in the
Middle East.
The ancient inhabitants were the old Phoenicians who
used the cedars of Lebanon to build boats which they sailed throughout
the length and breadth of the Mediterranean.
Lebanon was the base used
by the early Crusaders against the infidels in attempts to capture
the Holy Land.
In fact, the people of Lebanon are still predominently
Christian.
However, they join the 40% Moslem population in hatred of
the Jews.
You will note on the enclosed map, which is a new one just
off the press,
that Israel is not shown.
One of our fellow passengers
is a brother of King Abdul of Trans-Jordan.
The latter you will re-
member was the leader of the Arabs in their struggle with the Jews.
That war may flare up again at any time, but I suspect that Lebanon
will not be drawn into it.
Saturday
March 25, 1950
En route Damascus-Brussels
At Beirut I tended to some business while Debby and Hebe
We attended the first anniversary cocktail party of Middle
East Airlines; also a small dinner party.
They should celebrate.
Their earnings for the first year were 800,000 Lebanon pounds on a
capital of 1,200,000 pounds (about three to one U.S. dollar). We left
by car at 7:00 this morning for the three-hour drive to Damascus.
two countries have a Customs Union, with Beirut serving as the only
port, but Syrie is now claiming more than its heretofore allotted 65%
share of the customs revenue.
It's quite a wrangle but not too un-
friendly.
Syria has a coastline as iong as that of Lebanon, but no
port and it would cost more than the Syrians have got or can get to
build one.
So they threaten and bluff but the Lebanese sit back with
a Mona Lisa smile and keep on saying, "only 65%". Neutrals say the
division should really be 75-25.
At Damascus we learned that our good friends the Tegens
were on this plane and sure enough we ran into them at the airport.
In New York I serve as a director of Al Tegen's General Public Utilities
and we see each other about once e month. However, on this trip the
Tegens welcomed us with leis at Honolulu, again we met in Manila and now
- quite by chance - we're flying together from Damascus to Brussels.
Our flight path takes us over Cyprus, Rhodes (two more British strong
spots!) Turkey, Greece, Yugoslavie, Austria, Germany.
At Brussels Debby and Hebe will stay overnight and go on
to Paris in the morning either by air or rail, and I stay on this
airplane through to London.
It's the end of our present itinerary. As in the reading
of a good book you hate to see it come to an end, but in like manner
it is one of those interesting and pleasant experiences which you
put away on the shelves of your mental library with a feeling that
due to it life is a little more worthwhile.
Sincerely,
H.M.B.
